---
title: "Quiz: rotation and scale become shifts (Fourier–Mellin)"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Fourier–Mellin resamples the magnitude spectra of two images on a log-polar grid, where rotation and scale are shifts, and finds them by phase correlation.

---

**Q1.** Why does plain phase correlation fail when B is turned by 30°?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does a shift compare, and what does a turn do to the direction of the edges?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Phase correlation tests shifts only: it lines up the same structures side by side. After a turn, the edges and textures of B point in other directions than in A, so no shift makes them agree; the surface is a flat floor with no clear peak (in the lecture's example 0.05 instead of 0.83).
:::

---

**Q2.** You unwrap an image on a polar grid around a point and turn the image by 45° about that same point. What happens to the unwrapped picture?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each row is one circle around the point.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every row (every circle) moves along itself by 45°, the same number of columns for all rows, wrapping around at 360°. The rotation has become a circular shift of the columns.
:::

---

**Q3.** How can a single inverse FFT give the score of every angle when the rotational correlation adds up many rings?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The correlation theorem is linear.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each ring's circular correlation is the inverse FFT of $\overline{A_m}B_m$ of that ring. The inverse FFT is linear, so the sum of the rings' correlations is the inverse FFT of the **sum** of their products: add the products first (one FFT per ring per image), then transform back once.
:::

---

**Q4.** B is A turned and shifted, by an unknown amount about an unknown point. Which of the three changes does the magnitude spectrum $\lvert F\rvert$ keep, and which does it remove?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The shift theorem; and what happens to stripes when the image turns.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It removes the **shift** (a shift changes only the phases), and keeps the **turn**: $\lvert F_B\rvert$ is $\lvert F_A\rvert$ turned by the same angle about the centre of the spectrum, a centre that is always known. (A change of scale would show as a shrinking or growing spectrum.)
:::

---

**Q5.** Why are the radii of the grid spaced **logarithmically**?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does scaling by $s$ do to a radius, and what does the logarithm turn a product into?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Scaling the image by $s$ multiplies every radius of the spectrum by $1/s$. On a log scale a multiplication is an addition: $\ln(r/s) = \ln r - \ln s$. So the scale becomes a shift by $\ln s$ along the rows, which phase correlation can find, together with the turn along the columns.
:::

---

**Q6.** Fourier–Mellin reports a turn of 20°. Why must you also test 200°, and how?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What symmetry does the magnitude spectrum of a real image have?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\lvert F\rvert$ of a real image is point-symmetric (unchanged by a turn of 180°), so the log-polar step only knows the angle modulo 180°. Undo both 20° and 200° on B and phase-correlate each with A: the true one leaves a shifted copy of A and a high shift peak, the other a copy turned upside down and no peak.
:::

---

**Q7.** Without a taper, Fourier–Mellin says "no turn, scale 1" for two clearly turned, unevenly lit images. Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where are the jumps of a periodic image, and do they turn with the sample?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The FFT treats each image as periodic; the brightness jumps where the borders meet put a bright cross along the axes of $\lvert F\rvert$. The cross belongs to the frame, not to the sample, so it sits at 0° and 90° in both spectra, unturned and unscaled: it votes for "no turn, scale 1". A Hann taper removes the jumps.
:::

---

**Q8.** The high-pass weight on $\lvert F\rvert$ helps on clean images. When does it hurt?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which frequencies does it lift, and what lives there?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It damps the low frequencies and so gives the high ones more weight. Noise is spread evenly over all frequencies, so at high frequencies it is stronger than the image: on noisy images the high-pass lifts mostly noise and the peak drowns (in the demo: noise SD 25 fails with it and works without it).
:::

---

**Q9.** Give two situations where Fourier–Mellin is the wrong tool.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Think of the range of scales and of how much content the views share.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
For example: a scale change far outside about 0.5–2 (the pattern leaves the log-polar grid and the views share little content); two views that overlap only partly (the spectra describe different content); perspective or non-rigid changes (not a turn and a scale); a strongly periodic or nearly empty image (many or no peaks). Matching keypoints and fitting a transform handles the large and partial cases.
:::

---

**Q10.** *(math)* B is A turned by $\alpha$ and enlarged by $s$. In log-polar coordinates $(\rho, \theta)$ of the magnitude spectrum, by how much is B's pattern shifted, and what happens to the factor $s^2$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\lvert B(\mathbf k)\rvert = s^2\lvert A(sR_{-\alpha}\mathbf k)\rvert$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\lvert B\rvert(\rho, \theta) = s^2\lvert A\rvert(\rho + \ln s, \theta - \alpha)$: shifted by $+\alpha$ in angle and $-\ln s$ in $\rho$. The constant factor $s^2$ multiplies every value equally; phase correlation normalises each frequency to size 1, so it does not matter.
:::
